checked: Premise and conclusion are defined in the opening paragraph before deductive reasoning uses them. Assumption uses statement, not the undefined proposition.

Negation, deductive, infer, all, some, none, may, must, best-supported, motive, and bias are explained before their applications. A and B are explicitly parts of statements. No prerequisite explanation is needed.
Necessary assumptions are taught through the negate-and-test method and the helpful-versus-needed distinction. Each quantified or compound negation pattern states what makes the original false.
The strength-word list explains none as total exclusion and may as possibility. Examples 5 and 6 apply those meanings.
Best-supported selection has a four-step evidence comparison procedure and worked ranking in #7. Cause, motive, and bias each have an evidence criterion and a separate worked example.
The negation test is limited to the argument's stated reason and does not require the assumption to prove the conclusion alone. Inclusive or is explicitly distinguished from an exclusive reading.

Some may include all; may is not certainty; deductive conclusions assume true premises. Observed patterns are limited to observed cases, association alone does not establish cause, and sequence alone does not establish motive.
Bias requires evidence beyond having an opinion or omitting material from a short passage. Best-supported choices must have actual support, even when cautiously worded.

lesson-verbal-logic-assumptions-and-conc.quote: Negate (B): at least one employee cannot access the website notices. That employee would lose access, so the stated reason fails.
lesson-verbal-logic-assumptions-and-conc.note: The overpass example is replaced by a necessary access condition for replacing printed notices. The negation defeats the stated access requirement.
Example 7 now requires choosing the supported appointment/wait link and compares it with overbroad and causal claims.

lesson-verbal-logic-assumptions-and-conc.quote: Choose the answer with the closest match to the evidence and the fewest unsupported claims.
lesson-verbal-logic-assumptions-and-conc.note: A four-step method now explains how to compare evidence and remove unsupported additions; example 7 applies it.

lesson-verbal-logic-assumptions-and-conc.quote: Test the reason the argument gives, not a new reason you can imagine.
lesson-verbal-logic-assumptions-and-conc.note: The diagnostic-heuristic sentence has been replaced with a short direct instruction.

lesson-verbal-logic-assumptions-and-conc.quote: It may be likely without being certain.
lesson-verbal-logic-assumptions-and-conc.note: The former abstract contrast is now explained in plain words and followed by a concrete selection method.
Example 3 now includes an explicit question after the premises and before its solution.

lesson-verbal-logic-assumptions-and-conc.quote: An **assumption** is an unstated statement that the reasoning needs.
lesson-verbal-logic-assumptions-and-conc.note: The definition now uses statement and removes the undefined logic term proposition.

lesson-verbal-logic-assumptions-and-conc.quote: A **premise** is a statement given as a reason or fact.
lesson-verbal-logic-assumptions-and-conc.note: Premise is defined in the opening paragraph before any deductive rule uses the plural premises.

lesson-verbal-logic-assumptions-and-conc.quote: **None** means no members. If no inspectors are trainees, any known inspector is not a trainee.
lesson-verbal-logic-assumptions-and-conc.note: None receives an exclusion rule; may receives a possibility rule. Separate worked examples apply each meaning.

reasoning-verbal-logic#7.quote: Check which parts of each choice those facts support.
reasoning-verbal-logic#7.note: The four-step ranking method and example 7 compare passage evidence with each conclusion and limit scope.

reasoning-verbal-logic#9.quote: They do not rule out other causes. They also give no visitors' reasons.
reasoning-verbal-logic#9.note: Example 8 applies the cause check to a before/after change and selects the recorded change without causal attribution.

reasoning-verbal-logic#10.quote: Separate the action from its possible reasons. Carlo read the feedback and then approved the schedule.
reasoning-verbal-logic#10.note: Example 9 separates the recorded action from fear and impressing others, which lack supporting evidence.

reasoning-verbal-logic#14.quote: Joel is contract staff. Therefore, **Joel is not a permanent employee**.
reasoning-verbal-logic#14.note: Example 5 applies the none-class exclusion to a named member and derives the required negative conclusion.

reasoning-verbal-logic#15.quote: Only **(C)** keeps the meaning of the statement.
reasoning-verbal-logic#15.note: Example 6 compares certainty, impossibility, and possibility. The solution preserves the meaning of may.

reasoning-verbal-logic#17.quote: Negate the whole statement: **the scanner does not work or the network is not available**. Either failure makes the original statement false.
reasoning-verbal-logic#17.note: Core Concept lists quantified and compound negation rules. Examples 10 and 11 apply all and conjunction negation and explain their effect.

reasoning-verbal-logic#19.quote: Look for unfair praise or blame, facts chosen to show only one side, or claims accepted without support.
reasoning-verbal-logic#19.note: The lesson defines bias criteria and example 12 identifies unfair blame and missing supporting facts.

lesson-verbal-logic-assumptions-and-conc.quote: A necessary assumption does not have to prove the conclusion alone.
lesson-verbal-logic-assumptions-and-conc.note: The lesson now uses only the reduced reasoning layout. Examples lead directly into traps with no Speed Tricks section.

lesson-verbal-logic-assumptions-and-conc.quote: The company could check completion on paper. The promised promotions could still happen.
